title: Mandatory Palestine
wiki_lead:
Mandatory Palestine, officially known as Palestine, was a British administrative territory in the region of Palestine between 1920 and 1948. Under the League of Nations mandate system, Britain was entrusted with administrating Palestine on the development of representative institutions and eventual self-government. From 1922, Britain administered the territory under the Mandate for Palestine with the British High Commissioner under the Colonial Office as its chief administrator. 
After the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire during the First World War in 1916, British forces drove Ottoman forces out of the Levant between 1917 and 1918. For the British, the United Kingdom had agreed in the McMahon–Hussein Correspondence that it would honour Arab independence in case of a revolt but, in the end, the United Kingdom and France divided what had been Ottoman Syria under the Sykes–Picot Agreement—an act of betrayal in the eyes of the Arabs. Another issue that later arose was the Balfour Declaration of 1917, in which Britain promised its support for the establishment of a Jewish "national home" in Palestine.  The declaration effectively overrode the emerging principle of self-determination for the territory's existing Palestinian Arab population. Mandatory Palestine was then established in 1920, and the British obtained a Mandate for Palestine from the League of Nations in 1922. Mandatory Palestine was designated as a Class A Mandate, based on its social, political, and economic development. This classification was reserved for post-war mandates with the highest capacity for self-governance. All Class A mandates other than Mandatory Palestine had gained independence by 1946.
At the formal beginning of the Mandate, the population was approximately 11% Jewish, 9% Christian Arab, and 78% Muslim Arab. During the Mandate, the area saw successive waves of Jewish immigration and the rise of nationalist movements in both the Jewish and Arab communities. Competing interests of the two populations led to the 1936–1939 Arab revolt in Palestine and the 1944–1948 Jewish insurgency in Mandatory Palestine. The United Nations Partition Plan for Palestine, adopted by the UN General Assembly in November 1947, recommended dividing the territory into two states, one Arab and one Jewish. The 1948 Palestine war ended with the territory of Mandatory Palestine divided among the State of Israel, the Hashemite Kingdom of Transjordan, which annexed territory on the West Bank of the Jordan River, and the Kingdom of Egypt, which established the "All-Palestine Protectorate" in the Gaza Strip.

Etymology

The name given to the Mandate's territory was "Palestine", in accordance with local Palestinian Arab and Ottoman usage and with European tradition. The Mandate charter stipulated that Mandatory Palestine would have three official languages: English, Arabic and Hebrew.

grok_lead: Mandatory Palestine was a British-administered geopolitical entity in the Levant from 1920 to 1948, established under the League of Nations Mandate for Palestine to prepare the territory for self-governing institutions while facilitating the establishment of a Jewish national home, as outlined in the incorporated 1917 Balfour Declaration, and safeguarding the civil and religious rights of all inhabitants. The mandate territory initially encompassed lands both west and east of the Jordan River, but Transjordan (known today as Jordan) was separated in 1922â1923 as a semi-autonomous emirate under Abdullah I, leaving Mandatory Palestine proper as the approximately 26,000 square kilometers west of the Jordan, corresponding to modern-day Israel, the West Bank, and Gaza Strip. The period saw substantial Jewish immigration, rising from about 11% of the population in 1922 to over 30% by 1947, driven by Zionist settlement and later flight from European antisemitism, fostering economic modernization including industry, agriculture, and infrastructure development under British oversight. Yet, this demographic shift and land purchases fueled Arab opposition, manifesting in communal violence such as the 1920â1921 riots, 1929 disturbances, and the sustained Arab Revolt (1936â1939), which prompted British military suppression and policy reversals like the restrictive 1939 White Paper limiting Jewish immigration and land acquisition amid World War II constraints. Postwar pressures, including Holocaust survivors seeking refuge and irreconcilable Arab-Jewish demands, led Britain to relinquish the mandate to the United Nations in 1947. The UN Special Committee proposed partitioning the territory into separate Jewish and Arab states with internationalized Jerusalem. This plan was accepted by Jewish leaders but rejected by Arab states and Palestinian representatives, escalating civil conflict. The mandate formally terminated at midnight on May 14â15, 1948, as declared by the British government, triggering the Israeli Declaration of Independence and the immediate invasion by neighboring Arab armies, marking the onset of the 1948 ArabâIsraeli War and the de facto division of the territory.
